title: Delicate token shepherd and KV prioritization for graceful OOM recovery
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem statement: Production clusters occasionally hit transient OOMs during wide sequence-length spikes and heterogeneous request mixes. These OOMs manifest as hard failures or long tail latency as the runtime stalls and attempts naive spill/evict strategies. Current mitigations (basic eviction + single-model fallback) reduce frequency but cause sharp quality drops and unpredictable latency for premium customers.

Goal: Implement a low-latency, low-quality-regression OOM prevention and recovery flow that combines continuous batch admission trimming, token-level KV prioritization, and a minimal-cost micro-fallback path. This flow should: 1) prevent or reduce hard OOMs by adapting admission and KV residency proactively, 2) degrade model fidelity gracefully when necessary, 3) provide clear observability and retriable recovery semantics for callers.

Scope: Engine + admission controller + routing. Not in scope: billing model changes, data-plane encryption changes.

Technical approach summary:
- Token shepherd score: compute a lightweight per-request priority score at admission using features (customer tier, request age, prefix hit-rate, live KV residency size, estimated token delta). Use score to decide: a) priority of keeping request's KV materialized, b) batch trimming order when under memory pressure.
- Sliding KV priority windows: maintain LRU-like tiers but with probabilistic retention that favors requests with near-term re-use (prefix cache hits) and high customer tier. When memory headroom drops below thresholds, trim low-score KV segments first (coalesced trimming to avoid thrash).
- Continuous batch admission trimming: instead of dropping entire requests, dynamically reduce batch size by trimming trailing tokens from low-score requests (soft-fidelity drop) and let high-score requests keep full context. This reduces peak KV footprint while preserving overall useful work.
- Fast micro-fallback: pre-warm a tiny quantized micro-model (e.g., 125M - 350M) on the same GPU/host in a keep-alive slot. When a request cannot be admitted with acceptable KV retention, route the request to the micro-model with a jittered retry back to the full model once headroom recovers. Provide structured response metadata indicating fallback and confidence delta.
- Async host spill and quiet reclaim: for long-tail pressure, asynchronously spill cold KV segments to host memory with a bounded async reclaim window. Prioritize reclamation for upcoming high-score requests.
- Circuit breaker + hedging: detect pathological tails (repeated OOM cycles) and enable a short-lived global batch contraction and increased micro-fallback ratio to stabilize the cluster.

Trade-offs considered:
- Complexity vs predictability: Token-level scoring and probabilistic KV retention increases runtime complexity and observability surface; we mitigate by strict telemetry and conservative defaults.
- Quality vs uptime: Soft trimming preserves partial outputs but reduces per-request completion fidelity; fallback to micro-model trades fidelity for latency and predictable success.
- Resource cost: Keeping a micro-model warm consumes slot budget; we restrict warm micro-models to a small fraction of GPU slots and enable region-specific opt-in.

Progress updates (chronological):
- 2026-01-28 — Ticket created. Initial problem framing and owner assigned.
- 2026-02-04 — Proto: implemented token score computation and unit tests; bench harness shows 12% reduction in peak KV bytes for synthetic long-prefix workload. (PR 7860)
- 2026-02-15 — Added probabilistic KV trimming and coalesced eviction window; observed oscillation on mixed-tenant canary. Investigation pointed to synchronized trimming windows causing thrash.
- 2026-02-22 — Mitigation: added jittered trimming offsets and score hysteresis; thrash reduced in canary.
- 2026-02-28 — Integrated fast micro-fallback support and structured response metadata. Micro-model warmed with adaptive keepalive policy.
- 2026-03-04 — Canary: 72-hour run on two clusters. Observed 58% reduction in hard OOM incidents, P95 latency spike frequency down 43% for affected tenants. Micro-fallback used in ~1.7% of requests (mostly ultra-long sequences). Dashboard link above.
- 2026-03-09 — Review with PM & SRE: agreed to wider canary and add graceful-rollout flags. Requested more end-to-end tests and customer-facing observability fields.

Open implementation tasks:
- Finish integration tests for async host spill and reclaim (ENG-84711-T1).
- Add per-tenant configuration and RBAC guardrails for micro-model warm slots (ENG-84711-T2).
- Create console observable tiles (token-score distribution, KV residency heatmap, fallback attribution) and add to rollout dashboard (ENG-84711-T3).
- Add end-to-end quantized-micro-model quality delta benchmarks and docs for SDK teams (ENG-84711-T4).

Testing & validation plan:
- Unit: score computation, hysteresis, trimming window correctness.
- Integration: admission controller with runtime; simulate heavy-tail sequences, verify no OOMs and expected trimming behavior.
- Canary: staged rollout (10% -> 30% -> 60%) across clusters with guardrail that blocks if customer_error_rate or OOMs increase.
- SLO verification: ensure P95 latency increase <= 15% for routes enabled; number of hard OOMs reduced by >= 40% vs baseline.

Review feedback and decisions:
- PM (Liang Chen): requested explicit SDK metadata for fallbacks so customers can detect and optionally rerun requests. Decision: include response header and structured JSON field with fallback_reason and fallback_model_id.
- Design (Megan O'Connor): asked for UX wording around 'soft-trim' quality degradation. Decision: surface both token_count_trimmed and estimated_quality_delta in console and API.
- SRE (Ravi Anand): required kill-switch flag per-cluster and an auto-rollback policy if memory pressure increases beyond threshold. Implemented.

Acceptance criteria (must be met before marking Done):
- Automated integration tests showing no hard OOMs under synthetic heavy-tail load (pass).
- Canary run stable for 72h with OOM reduction >= 40% and P95 latency regression <= 15%.
- Console tiles added and populated in canary clusters.
- Documentation: Confluence design doc updated, SDK changelog entry and example for inspecting fallback metadata.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 1: internal canary on non-prod clusters (complete).
- Phase 2: opt-in customers and non-critical prod routes (10% traffic) — monitor 48h.
- Phase 3: broader production rollout with per-tenant opt-out and telemetry (target after 2 successful opt-in waves).

Next steps for assignee:
- Complete ENG-84711-T1 and T2 by 2026-03-17.
- Prepare a short demo for the weekly runtime sync (2026-03-11).

Notes and follow-ups:
- Consider future work to combine token shepherding with model-aware kernel-selection so that trimmed batches pick the most efficient kernels.
- Track customer feedback channels for any quality complaints; set up an automatic triage label for fallback-attributed requests.
